Mr* J. A. C. ETHIER (Two Mountains). (Translation.) Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are called I rise to call your attention to a matter which concerns me personally and which is in the nature of a matter of privilege. Here are the facts
which I wish to bring to the attention of the House : On Monday, March 18, I as a member of this House and within my right as such, prepared and placed in the hands of the Clerk of this House the following question :-
1.	Is the government aware that, since the beginning of the present session, the translators of the Debates have each day translated into English all the French, and into French all the English by them received for that purpose from the Government Printing Bureau, notwithstanding that the amount of matter for translation is equivalent at times to as much as 128 columns of Hansard, in a single day ?
2.	Is the government aware that since the opening of the present session, the translators of the Debates have also corrected and returned to the Printing Bureau each day, all the proofs sent to them therefrom for that purpose, notwithstanding that such proofs amount at times to as much as 125 columns of Hansard, in a single day ?
3.	Is the government aware that, up to this date (March 18), the Bureau has sent to the translators of the Debates, matter for translation up to the 12th only, and proofs for correction up to the 11th only ; and that of the French version it has paged and published the Debates up to the beginning of the sitting of March 4 only, notwithstanding that the amount of matter for translation in the hands of the printer is sufficient to bring the work up to the 14th at least, and the paging and publishing up to the 11th ?
4.	Is the government aware that the delay in the printing and distributing of the French Hansard is due to the management of the Printing Bureau and not to the translators of the Debates, who labour day by day and even Sundays and holidays, if necessary, in order to translate forthwith as it is received, all matter furnished to them ?
5.	Is the government aware that the delays and tardiness of the Government Printing Office in printing the French edition of. the Hansard, is the means of depriving the representatives of the people, the press and the public in general of the advantages they should derive from the steady labour of the translators ?
6.	Is it the intention of the Government to put a stop to the delay caused by the Printing Bureau and to secure the paging and publishing, in due time, of the French edition of the House of Commons Debates ?
This question was placed on tbe Order paper and it still stands there in my name. It will probably be put on Monday, when comes tbe time for calling it. It seems that, this question has started quite a controversy this week.

Let me first quote from the last paragraph of an editorial of La Patrie, of March 11th, in reply to two editorials which had appeared in the columns of Le Journal, on the 27tli of February, and on the 8tli instant, respectively. This article, under the heading :	' The Translation of the Debates,'
winds up as follows :-
Le Journal lays the blame on the government and makes it still more responsible for that condition of affairs than the translating staff. The matter ought to be throughly sifted and probed to the bottom once for all, and Justice should be given to whom Justice Is due.
Now, on the 20th instant after this question had been placed on the Order paper and printed, La Patrie, in its daily parliamentary correspondence, struck the right note about the merits of this question.
But on the 21st, that same paper, not in its parliamentary correspondence but in an editorial under the heading :
' The Hansard trouble,' referring to my absence from the House-for, as a matter of fact, ou Monday night I was absent from the House, and in so doing, I have only been using a common privilege to all members of this House, and for which I do not think I am called upon to offer any excuse or explanation. Mr. Ethier being absent from the House yesterday, his question in connection with Hansard *was dropped.

House resumed adjourned debate on the proposed motion of Hon. Mr. Fielding :
That Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into committee to consider of the Ways and Means for raising the Supply to be granted to His Majesty; and the proposed motion of Mr. Borden (Halifax) in amendment thereto.
['I dissent.']

Mr. Speaker, as the announcements of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) necessarily cover every department of the fiscal and commercial policy and administration of the country, it is only reasonable that the discussion of these announcements should wander far and wide, a privilege which has been very fully availed of by, I think, most of the hon. members who have taken part in the discussion so far. But, while our discussion may cover a great deal of ground, our vote is narrowed down to the point of whether we shall endorse the policy and administration expressed by these announcements, or whether we shall accept the resolution in amendment of the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax). In deciding which of these motions we shall support it is not necessary, nor is it possible, that we should all absolutely agree with either the one or the other. In any country, and particularly in a country so widespread as Canada, there must necessarily be many points of view in regard to the policy of taxation, the trade policy and the fiscal policy of the country. I assume that members are elected to parliament for the purpose of representing those several interests and sections, not
by endeavouring to force absolutely their particular views upon the whole House so much as to, as far as possible, find a common ground upon which they can stand to work together for the common good. I hope, then, that in discussing the budget from the point of view of the interests of the locality which I am particularly identified with, I will not be accused of any greater lack of patriotism, or any great sectionalism than any other hon. member, representing other interests, may be accused of. In discussing the question of taxation raised by means of a tariff, we find that the full meaning and purport of the taxation is not represented merely by the rate of duty nor by the average rate of duty. A certain level percentage rate of duty levied on all articles alike would be eminently unfair to those classes of the community who would be affected by the tariff through their purchases of necessities rather than of luxuries. A 10 per cent duty on everything would be a greater burden upon the community at large than a 30 per cent duty might be if applied to certain articles. So, too, on the protective side of the tariff because a tariff, in so far as it is a tariff, must necessarily be that far protective,-or, possibly, destructive-those industries which depend on an export market for their ultimate prosperity cannot by any possibility derive the same advantage from the protective features of the tariff as those industries which depend on the home market. So, there are very wide differences in the point of view both in regard to taxation and in regard to protection. I need not tell the hon. members of this House that in that part of Canada lying west of Lake Superior the purchase of necessities is immeasurably greater than the purchase of luxuries. I need not say that that part of Canada depends on the advantages it receives in the export market rather than on the advantages it receives in the home market for its ultimate success. Therefore, west of Lake Superior, the conditions of the country are favourable to low taxation on necessaries and low protection ; in other words, the country west of Lake Superior is, in its own interest, necessarily a low tariff country. I need not say that the country west of Lake Superior is not the only part of Canada that is so interested. Wherever, in all this broad Dominion, the majority of the people are buying necessaries instead of luxuries, and wherever, in this broad Dominion, the prosperity of the producer depends upon exports rather than upon home sales, their position is necessarily the same as that of the country west of Lake Superior, and their interests are also identified with a low tariff.
In so far as the tariff which has been put in force by the present administration is concerned; in so far as that tariff has given to the consuming and export producing class of this country relief from the burdens

which they formerly bore, in so far it necessarily has our support. In so far as it has not clone that it necessarily must meet with our criticism. There are features of the present tariff which some of us do not consider satisfactory. We believe that there are articles upon which the tariff is unfairly high, and if it were possible for us to secure a reduction in these particulars we would take such means as would be necessary to secure that reduction. Having recognized the advantages which we have derived under the present tariff policy and administration; having stated the points on which we feel inclined to criticise that policy, the question for us to decide is ; Where do we stand or how do we stand in regard to the alternative proposition placed before us by the leader of the opposition ? Is it to that proposition that we are to look for greater advantages than we enjoy under the tariff policy of the present administration ? I will not read the amendment to the House, because the House is no doubt familiar with it. It is divided into three paragraphs, and if I might be allowed to give my poor judgment in regard to the meaning of those paragraphs, I would say that paragraph No. 1 declares for a protective tariff for all industries in Canada ; that paragraph No. 2 declares for trade advantages to be given to all parts of the empire, and that paragraph No. 3 declares for a tariff war against all the rest of the world. For my part I am a protectionist in principle and in practice. I believe that it is the business of auy government to protect the interest of the country over which it is called to govern, and if the leader of the opposition or if his friends behind him can show me a reasonable means whereby he can protect and advantage the labouring, the agricultural, the manufacturing, the mining and other industrial interests in Canada by a tariff adjustment, he can have my vote.
Hear, hear.

But judged in the light of past events; judged in the light of the events transpiring in this country since the adoption of the so-called protective tariff in 1878; our experience leads us to believe that so-called national protection means protection for one class and one interest of the community, and the sacrifice of every other.
Hear, hear.

It will be for our friends opposite to explain in what way they propose to advance the agricultural and mining interests of the west by changes in the tariff. They have not attempted to do so yet. and we would be glad to hear from them on that point. The so-called protective tariff; the mis-called national policy was framed in 1878. It was framed, we are given to understand, by a master hand and by a master mind; but that policy Mr. OLIVER.
framed by a master mind and administered by a master hand never did give protection to the agricultural and mining interests of Canada any more than it did to any of the other of these interests and industries which depended upon the export market for their success.
As to the policy of mutual trade preference within the empire, I would be glad to know how our friends propose to adequately protect every interest within Canada, and at the same time provide for a trade preference throughout the empire. Do they propose to get something for nothing ? The world has changed, if they can get a preference throughout the empire without giving something in return. And then I ask them : What interest which they have pledged themselves here to absolutely and adequately protect, are they going to sacrifice, and to what measure are they going to sacrifice it, in order to secure this mutual trade preference throughout the empire? I would ask them further : What they propose to do about the trade preference that exists at the present time between Great Britain and Canada. I understand that our friends on the other side are not in favour of that trade preference, although they have not specifically declared themselves against it. We would like them to come off the fence and say just exactly what they are going to do about it, because I would like them to understand that the principle of preferential trade with Britain as it stands at the present time appeals to the views and the interests of that section of the people of Canada who depend upon the export market of Great Britain for their ultimate success. Under the present preference, we who depend for our success upon the export of our products believe that any measure that tends to improve our market in Britain is a benefit to us, and when we secure that preference in the British market, not by giving something, but by taking something-that is, the privilege of buying what we want at a lower rate of duty-I say that preference is good enough for us until we can get something better at any rate, and it has our endorsation not only as a matter of sentiment, but as a matter of practical business. In regard to the third paragraph of the amendment which declares for a tariff war with the world, I would ask again: If we are to regulate our tariff, not as is stated in the first paragraph for the purpose of protecting every interest within our country, but for the purpose of attacking every Interest in every other country. It seems to me that there is as great difficulty in meeting both conditions as between the first and third paragraph as between the first and second. I believe in the principle of regulating our tariff according to our own needs and requirements and in our own interests I do not think it is a principle capable of general application that whenever any other
189(3'
country sees fit to put up a certain tariff against us, we should therefore put up the same tariff against it. For these reasons, while I still criticise the fiscal policy of the government and their administration in any particular wherein I consider they have not done the best that can he done for the well-being of the part of the country in which I am most deeply interested, I am compelled to vote for the resolution of the government instead of that of the opposition.
The amendment of the leader of the opposition is a statement of policy on the part of a great political party, a party which hopes again to rule the destinies of this country ; and I would be glad to understand exactly what is meant by what is said. When the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) was replying to the speech of the Finance Minister, he criticised the fiscal policy of the government, and it seemed to me with fairly good reason. He said that he thought a time when the revenues were swelling was a time when either the taxation should be reduced or the debt decreased. He said that in his speech, but it is not embodied in this resolution. I ask you to reconcile if you can the wording of the first paragraph of the resolution, which declares for pronounced and adequate protection, or in other words high duties, with the statement of the hon. member for West Toronto that a rising revenue should be accompanied by reduced taxation. If hon. gentlemen opposite will give us a policy which will appeal to the interests and provide for the well-being of the great producing industries and the great consuming classes of this country, then they can have the support of the representatives of those classes and those interests. But so long as they see fit to declare in this House, if not in resolution, at any rate in speech, that every interest of this vast country is governed by and involved in the one single and minor interest of manufacturing, just so long must they depend on the manufacturing interest for their support, and just so long will I take the liberty of returning to them the accusation of sectionalism and narrowness which has been levelled on several occasions in this House against the representatives of the western country, because they upheld western interests. I wish it to he always understood that the people of the west have no animosity towards the manufacturing interests. We wish them nothing 'but an abundant success. We are not sectionaliists. , We like to see this eastern Canada built up ; we are proud when we see it prospering. We like to see these tall chimneys rising ; we like to see those thousands of people employed in manufacturing ; we like to see those great pay rolls. That is one side of the question. But we do not like to see gentlemen 00
who represent the manufacturing interest stand up in this House and assume and declare that the manufacturing interest must be protected at all hazards, and that every other interest is secondary to that-thatf the prosperity of this country is dependent on whether those gentlemen get a cent more or a cent less on their cottons and their woollens. So long as we are levying our taxation by means of the tariff, just so long are these gentlemen entitled to all the incidental protection which a revenue tariff will give them. They are more than heartily welcome to it, and any success which they can achieve under these conditions we shall rejoice to see them achieve. There is no sectionalism in that respect. But we are told-I have heard it stated from the front benches of the opposition- that so soon as any manufacturing industry is found to be languishing, then is the time to increase the tariff. The trouble with the manufacturers of Canada-if I may be allowed to be a judge-is that they have been living rather on the strength of the tariff than on the merits of their own case; and it is a happy thing for this country, instead of this being a time when one or more manufacturers can come down here and get another- turn of the tariff screw in order to help them out, the time has come when these gentlemen have to stand on their own feet and fight out their own salvation, just as we in the North-west have to do. If any particular industry cannot maintain itself under the protection accorded to it by a fair revenue tariff, then let the industry be chahged ; just as in the North-west, when wheat raising becomes unprofitable, we are told from every platform, in every newspaper and from every seat in parliament : Go into mixed farming. In the same way, if certain manufacturing industries cannot thrive under a revenue tariff, it is time for them to change to some other line of manufacture, instead of coming down to this House and putting themselves in the position of mendicants on our handis.
I do not want to go into a very extensive discussion of this question ; but one thing has attracted my attention in the plea which has always been put up on behalf of high duties in favour of the manufacturers. Whenever a demand Is made for a high duty in favour of the manufacturers, or whenever an attempt is made to reduce a duty, these gentlemen of the manufacturing industries forthwith barrica&e themselves behind a breastwork of petticoats and pinafores. It is the wives and children of their operatives who are going to be injured by any change in the tariff ; and an appeal is made to humanity when no other ground exists to keep up the tariff. But when the tariff is kept up. when it is thought advisable to form one of these great combines or trusts, when

lb 91

business gets a little slack, or when somebody is making a big donation for a public library or something of the kind, and a cut -is made in wages, we do not then hear ^anything about the suffering of the workmen or operatives in the factories.
Might I give a suggestion to these philanthropists who are so very anxious about their labouring men. Labouring men depend upon the necessaries of life the same as everybody else, and have less money with which to buy them. We have all heard about the iniquity with regard to coal oil, about the high duties on coal oil, and a good many of us believe that they are altogether too high. W coal oil is an article which absorbs a large part of the wages of these unfortunate operatives, but I have never yet seen or heard of a manufacturing association of Canada, or any representative of such associations, getting up in parliament and advocating a reduction of the duty on that article. No danger of their doing that, because that would be attacking the sacred principle of protection. It is with them a case of hang together, for if they do not hang together they will hang separately, and they support the duty on coal oil and every other high duty simply on the principle that the duties must be kept up, although it takes money out of the pockets of the operatives, which these operatives need so much.
The claim is made that the present tariff is the same as the old one. that the tariff policy of the present government is the same old national*policy of the late government. If it is, why move this resolution ? Why not endorse the policy of the government by accepting the motion of the lion. Minister of Finance ? I assume that in moving tiiis motion, lion, gentlemen opposite acknowledge that there is not only a radical difference between the tariff policy of the present government and that of the late government, but that the tariff policy of the present opposition differs from that of the present government, and differs because it does not give higher protection to manufacturing industries. If the resolution does not mean that, then it does not mean anything. [DOT]
Another side of the question I would like to touch, and one I have not heard dealt with yet. is with regard to the great prosperity which has flowed over this country during the past four or five years. I read from the speech of the hon. the Finance Minister :
But In summing up the affairs of the country, we are able to describe it as one of unexampled prosperity. Prosperity in trade and manufactures has brought prosperity to our national finances, and enables me at the close of the year to announce results which, it is not too much to say, form the most satisfactory financial statement that ever fell to the lot of a Minister of Finance to make in the Dominion of Canada. At a time of very considerable Mr. OLIVER.
financial stringency, at a time, too, when our expenditures were being conducted on a very liberal scale, we found our revenues so generous that we were able to provide for all our needs without having to resort to fresh loans, or even to an issue of treasury bills.
I want to call the attention of the House to the statement, which has not been challenged, that we are to-day financially and commercially in a most exceptionally prosperous condition, and the question arises, is that condition likely to continue ? If it is, we are to be congratulated. If it is not, we are to some extent to be deplored. The hon. the Finance Minister deals with that question as follows :
I think we have probably now reached about the crest of the wave of prosperity. I do not expect that we shall have any serious reverses.
think the business of Canada has been developed during the past four or five years upon very safe and sound lines. I think there has been, to a very large extent, an absence of that inflation which is so apt to mark a period of good times. I am of opinion that the business of the country as a whole has been so carefully conducted and is on such a sound basis that we are not likely to suffer any serious reverse, but I do not think it is reasonable to expect that we can go on increasing our business as rapidly as we have during the past few years. What may happen is that we might suffer a check.
I would be very sorry, Mr. Speaker, to hold out false liopes with regard to the future prosperity of our country. If we are liable to suffer a check, it is desirable that we should know it beforenand and prepare for it. and certainly the Minister of Finance is entitled to every credit for his prudence in calling attention to that unfortunate possibility. That point I propose to discuss in a few minutes, but the question I propose to consider now is, whence comes this great prosperity, because upon the source of that prosperity depends its continuance. That is a point which has not been fully brought out in this debate. Our prosperity comes not from the fact that we have been doing business, but from the fact that we have been doing an increased business. It is In the fact of the increase that our prosperity lies, and it is on the question as to whether that increase will continue or not. that the continuance of our prosperity depends. Where did this increase in trade come from ? Did it come by accident ? Did it drop from the clouds ? Where did it come from ? Have the farmers of Ontario produced so very much more crops during the past four years than during the preceding four years as to account for our increased export trade to the amount. I think, of $155,500,000 ? Is it due to the increase in our lumbering industry ? Is it due to the increase in our fisheries and our manufactures? No doubt there has been an increase, and a very satisfactory and desirable increase, in those lines. There is no doubt that the sound administration of the Finance Minister, and his
sound policy, have aided In increasing the general trade of the country a very considerable number of millions of dollars. But, I submit, not to the extent of $155,500,000 in the period of four years. Where does that increase come from ? X claim that the increase of trade within the past four or five years is due to the development of the country west of Lake Superior. From there and only from there could that stupendous increase come, and from there and from there only did it come. I feel constrained to dwell upon this point particularly, because of certain slurs which I have heard cast in this House as to the propriety of certain acts and policy respecting that western country-not so much, 1 admit, in recent years as in former years. It was the accepted idea in the public life of Canada not so many years ago, that the development of the western country was a mill-stone around the neck of eastern Canada. And that idea, I am sorry to say, is held yet in a good many of the back townships of this eastern country. I draw attention to the fact that we are enjoying unexampled trade prosperity in Canada ; and I draw attention to the fact that the only possible source from which that unexampled trade prosperity could come was the development of the country west of Lake Superior.
May I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) if it was from there that the large increase or exportation ;n hams and bacon came, and also the increase in our export of wheat ?
Not the hams and bacon, but certainly the wheat.
And the cheese ?
No.
And the butter ?

Partly, but not altogether. I said that the improvement of conditions in eastern Canada did account for millions of dollars, under the wise administration and policy of the present government. I acknowledge that ; but, I ask, and I challenge the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule), did the increase in the exports of cheese and hams and bacon account for this increase of over $155,000,000 in our exports ?
A share of it.
Undoubtedly, but only a share of it.
The larger part of it.

Well, we will see about that later-for that is the very point. We do not wish, remember, to set up as sec-tionalists ; but, we will not accept the position that the country which is-I will not say the hope, it has been the hope for many years-the foundation of the prosperity that I Canada is enj'oying, prosperity that is keep-604
ing the factories of eastern Canada busy, and is causing this House to discuss day after day questions of transportation and terminal facilities-I say we will not accept the position that that country is a drawback or in any way a detriment to the welfare of Canada at large, or that any policy which tends toward the development of that country is not a good policy and a sound policy for the Dominion at large.
Nobody disputes that; there is no need to argue it.

I am glad to have the support of the hon. member (Mr. Sproule). I hope I shall be as successful with his colleagues on that side. Prosperity has come because of this increase, and the increase has come because of the western development-that is, the larger part of it. It is the exports that pay for the imports, and, when we find out where the exports come from, we know where our prosperity comes from. I find, on looking over the Finance Minister's statement, that our exports increased from 1899 to 1900 to the extent of about $32,000,000. I find that of that increase of $32,000,000, the increase in the products of the mine represented about $11,000,000. How much of that came from Madoc or Marmora ? I find that the increase in the export of animals and their products amounted to about $9,500,000. I find that the increase in the export of agricultural products amounted to about $4,500,000. That is to say, out of this total of $32,000,000, the increase in these three items represented $25,000,000 ; and I submit that of the increase in these three items the greater part necessarily and actually came from the country west of Lake Superior. No man can argue that the mining industries of the eastern country produced $11,000,000 more for export last year than in the preceding year. No man can argue that there was $9,500,000 more of animals and their products exported from eastern Canada than there was in the year previous. No man can argue that there was $4,500,000 more of agricultural products exported from eastern Canada than there was in the year previous. The greater part of this increase, necessarily and as a matter of fact, came from west of Lake Superior, and it was this increase of exports from that western country that, as I say. kept your factories going and your wholesale houses busy. This is the secret of your prosperity : and, inasmuch as the development of that western country is not ended, is only beginning, I believe that we are not necessarily at the end of an era of prosperity, but that, if a wise and careful policy is pursued, we shall find that we are but at the beginning of an era of prosperity which will grow greater even than the present.
I have given the increase of exports in three great lines. Now let us see the other side. I find that our exports of manufactures

1S96
increased about $2,500,000-a very desirable increase, an increase that we are pleased to see and that we are proud of, but an increase that was a result of the prosperity of the country rather than the cause of it. Our fishery exports increased by about $1,250,000. Our exports of the products of the forests increased uDout $1,500,000. These are interests and industries particularly connected with eastern Canada. We find that in these items our exports have been increased to the extent of about $5,250,000, as against an increase of about $25.000,000 in the products of the mine and the farm. Had we been depending, then, upon the pleasing and satisfactory increase which has taken place in these lines, while we should have had fairly good times, we should not have had the unexampled prosperity which the Minister of Finance speaks of so fully in his opening remarks, and which is beyond challenge or question. Not only lias there been an increase in our exports as between last year and the year before, but, taking the figures given us by the Finance Minister, we find that there has been an increase very much in the same proportion, in the period of four years from 1896 to 1900, as compared with the period from 1893 to 1896. As between these two periods the total increase of exports was $155,500,000. Of these exports $37,500,000 were of mines, and $83,750,000 were of farm and animal products, or a total of $125,250,000, of the products of the mine and of the farm. Manufactures increased $13,500,000, the products of the forest, $12,000,000, and the fisheries, $750,000. On the one side of the slate you have $121,250,000, and on the other side $26,250,000.
I claim that there is something more required in the administration of the public affairs of this country than mere tinkering with the tariff. The tariff is not everything, though I admit that the tariff is important, inasmuch as it touches every one in the matter of taxation. It affects, or Can be made to affect, every current of trade. I do not wish to minimize the importance of the tariff, but I do think its importance has been greatly exaggerated in discussions of this subject. From the figures! I have placed before this House, I think it is clear that a policy that will tend to the still greater development of the mining and agricultural interests of this country, which particularly belong to the country west of Lake Superior, is the policy which will maintain and increase our prosperity.
Now, as to whether this increase did come from west of Lake Superior or not, is a question I will briefly consider. Of course, we cannot separate, in the trade returns, that which came from one part of the country and that which came from another. It all goes out and all comes in through our great ports and our great wholesale centres, and everything coming in through these Mr. OLIVER.
ports is credited to such ports and to the provinces in which they are found. Therefore, we have to go to other sources for our information as to the increased production of the western country. I find from the speech of the Finance Minister that from 1897 to 1900 the government collected a royalty of $2,000,000 upon the gold output of the Yukon. That royalty was levied, supposedly, at a rate of 10 per cent on all the gold mined over, I think, $2,500 to each mine. Now, I do not throw any aspersion upon the honesty of the people of the Yukon, nor upon the ability of the officials there ; but I think if you will deduct the $2,500 exemptions, and if you will make a reasonable allowance for the dislike of people to pay royalty unless they are obliged to, and for the facility which the handling of gold allows to parties to escape the royalty, you will agree that $2,000,000 does not represent by any means 10 per cent of the total output of gold of the Yukon. Indeed, I think it does not represent more than 5 per cent of the actual output. There must have been not less than $40,000,000 of gold mined in the Yukon territory from 1897 to 1900, judging by the returns of the royalty collected. On that point I desire to say a word. I have heard it argued that because it did not cost $40,000,000 to mine the gold, that therefore the country did not profit to the amount of the gold mined. I can only say, as one who has some little knowledge of mining conditions, that the idea is a fallacy, and that the mining of $40,000,000 worth of gold in the Yukon territory does mean a transaction of not less than $40,000,000 worth of business in connection with the mining of that gold. It is an accepted principle that it costs a dollar to take out a dollar's worth of gold from the ground, and some think more than a dollar. If it were not so, gold would sometime become cheap ; but it is so, and any tnan who has gone into gold mining as a speculation-and I think some of my hon. friends opposite will bear me out in the statement-is aware that it often costs more to take out gold than the value of the gold itself. The way it works is this : The richer the mine the greater the rush of people to it, and therefore the greater the waste of money by those who have joined in the rush; and of this waste of money the country gets the benefit in trade. So that although it did not cost $40,000,000 to mine that $40.000,000 of gold that was taken out of the ground, there was $40,000,000 expended, because of that $40,000,000 taken out. and the trade of this country or of some other country benefited to that extent because of that gold being mined.
It has been said that the United States has benefited entirely by the trade of the Yukon, that Canada has only benefited by the royalty that has been levied. I find from the speech of the minister that the customs duties levied on goods entering the Yukon in those four years, is about $1,000,-
OOO. Now, that $1,000,000 of duty levied on goods brought into the Yukon is not the trade that Canada got-is not the benefit that Canada got. It is the trade which Canada did not get. Taking a 334 per cent duty, $1,000,000 of duty collected would mean $3,000,000 of outside trade, and the balance was Canadian trade, representing the turnover of our merchants, our manufacturers and our dealers in this country, and particularly in the eastern country. Because of those articles which paid the $1,000,000 duty I think I am safe in saying the greater part consisted of agricultural products from the western states. The manufactured articles which went into the Yukon in recent years, at any rate, have been essentially Canadian goods, and Canadian trade has benefited therefrom.
I find from the report of the Minister of Mines of British Columbia, dated June 30th, 1899, that the production of the mines has increased between 1895 and 1899 from $5,500,000 to $12,250,000. Now, just as in the jcase of the Yukon, so in the case of the mines of British Columbia. My hon. friends from British Columbia will pardon me for alluding to their province, but I think they will bear me out in saying that the rule which I have stated in regard to the Yukon holds good in a large measure in regard to the mines of British Columbia, and that for the $12,250,000 taken out in 1899 not less than $10,000,000 of trade was necessarily done in connection with the mining of that amount. 1 will not put it any higher. It may have been a great deal more, but it certainly was not any less.
Then, we come further east, and I find it difficult to get returns that will answer the questions raised by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule), but, on looking into the Statistical Year-Book for 1899,1 find the increase of crop in the province of Manitoba therein stated, and I find that there is a difference between the crop yield of 1890 and the crop yield of 1899 as between 32,000.000 bushels, and 59,000,000 bushels, a difference of 27,000.000 bushels, almost double in three years. I think my hon. friends from Manitoba and the North-west Territories will bear me out when I say that, although the production in the Territories is not yet as large, the proportionate increase is very much greater. So, the crop of Manitoba and the west has absolutely and actually doubled in the three years from 1890 to 1890. and that doubling has meant an increase in the crop of between thirty and forty million bushels of grain which is worth just that much money. Now, I ask you. whether, in this eastern country, it is "possible for such an increase to be shown. It is not that this eastern country is not a good country, that it is not one of the fairest countries that the sun shines on, that it is not one of the finest countries in the world, but the opportunity for expansion is not here that is there. There can not be the increase where there is not the opportunity, and if Canada is to increase in her prosperity as she has done, then we must look to the development of the country west of Lake Superior, on the prairies and in the mountains for the future great prosperity and development of Canada, and we must be prepared to support a policy designed to promote the development of the country. Allow me to say that I am not one of those who are always calling for government expenditures in order to secure development.
I believe that Wise expenditures are ofttimes necessary, but wise and judicious administration is just as necessary as any possible expenditure of actual money. We had large expenditures in the period from 1882 until 1896, we had liberal expenditures, but we did not have results because we did not have wise administration, and it is greatly because of the wiser administration in regard to that country that we have enjoyed since 1896 that this prosperity has come about. With a continuation of a wise policy -1 do not say that we have reached perfection by any means-with a continuation of an improved policy, we will have still greater prosperity, in that country and in this eastern country, from whence you must look to the west for your ultimate and final greatness and prosperity.
As other hon. members nave wandered far afield from the letter of the resolution, so, I may add a word which I do not consider afield at all, but, as a final conclusion to what I have already said in regard to this eastern and western question. It was a principle held by the late government that it was not good policy to aid the movement of people from one part of Canada to another, as they put it. That it was not good policy to aid the movement of people from eastern Canada to western Canada. And we find to some extent, in fact, to a large extent, that idea is followed by the present administration as well as by the present opposition. It is against that idea that I wish to argue upon the present occasion. I say that if you are to have development, you must have opportunity. If you are to have development, you must give opportunity. You cannot make bricks without straw, you cannot expect a man in eastern Canada who is confined to the limits of a fifty, sixty or a hundred acre farm, or who is trying to wring a living out of soil that will not and cannot be made to produce to add largely if at all to the wealth of the country. That man, let him be the best man there ever was in the world, cannot produce the results that will be of general benefit to this country, that he could produce were he to transfer his energies to a wider and better opportunity. There is, and has been the idea that the progress of the west meant the injury of the east. I have read to the House to-day and have shown on the authority of the hon. Minister of Finance that it is upon the progress of the west that the

progress of the east has depended, is depending and must necessarily depend. Then, I say, instead of standing by this idea that we must keep our people at home, that we must keep them fenced up in little, confined, rocky fields, in poor parts of the country, it is the interest of every man to induce people so circumstanced to change their situation and to fake advantage of the wider opportunities offered by the western country. We have looked in the past to outsiders to develop our western country. We have, under the late government and under the present government, expended large amounts of money and we have advocated large policies for the purpose of settling that western country from the outside. Let me, in this House, say that what that country is from Lake Superior to the Alaskan boundary, it is, principally because of the exertions, the abilities and energies of the people of eastern Canada who have gone there to make their homes and to build up a new and greater Canada. It is because of what has been done, by the people who have gone out there from your midst, here, and who, because of the wider opportunities, have achieved greater successes. It is because of their abilities and energies that this addition has been made to our finances and to our prosperity. You have not lost by their going, but you have gained and you will not lose by the further going of such people to that country and building up there a market for your manufacturers, building up a market for your wholesale dealers, and providing traffic for your lines of transportation and great ocean ports, as they cannot cooped up as they are in many parts of this eastern country wearing out their lives in trying to wring a living out of the soil under circumstances that cannot yield them, one. It is to our own people that we owe the development of our western country as far as it has gone, and now, when we see as we do see, the benefit that accrues to us from the development of that country, it is for us to unite and consider it, not as an outside place, but as part of a great Canada. It is our common interest to build up a country that will be great in the west and so be great in the east.
You may ask : What would you wish to have done in order to bring this about. I would wish to have a change in sentiment; I would wish to have our public men look at this matter in the light I have viewed it to-day. Instead of men of light and leading in this eastern country holding to the idea that they must keep their people at home in eastern Canada-keep them settled on some rocky strip of land in New Ontario or some such region, I would ask them to realize that our manufacturers require a market, that our wholesale dealers require a market, that our railways and our ports require traffic. And how can we get that traffic so well as by transplanting our people from insurmountable difficulties here, to Mr. OLIVER.
illimitable opportunities there. If we adopt such a policy, then, I say, we need not look for that check to our prosperity which the Minister of Finance has foreshadowed. There will we find a solution for the financial problems of this country ; there will we find a means to maintain and increase the prosperity which has so astonished us within the last four years. That prosperity did not come by accident. It came by hard toil, it came by enterprise, it came by sound judgment, it came by men who took risks, and it came from the efforts of men of our own blood and our own name who transferred their energies from this country in the east to that country in the west; the men who have built up our western country as far as it has gone, but who have only touched the fringe of that vast empire that lies between Lake Superior and the Pacific coast.

in this country, that a preference should he given in our markets to the products of the mother country on condition of getting some advantage in the markets of Great Britain. There is a little paragraph following what I have read, which, perhaps, I might read for the edification of the right hon. leader of the House (Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier). This is said by the Secretary of State for the Colonies :
The right hon. gentleman suggests that we should treat them differently. No ! If we are willing to accept this favour and to thank Canada for it, and to give a gold medal to her Prime Minister for having proposed it, then, I think that the next thing is for the Cobden Club to give a gold medal to Mr. Rhodes.
This aroused the ire of Hr. Courtney, Hr. Horley and others. Hr. Courtney gets out of the difficulty by saying that the right hon. gentleman who leads the government (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) is something of an orator, but that he does not understand the principles of political economy :
What my right hon. friend says is this: that as between different divisions of the same political organization-the British Empire

This, it will be seen, is the interpretation that Mr. Courtney puts upon the words of the Secretary of State for the Colonies.
-there is no departure from free trade, although there is differential treatment of one part of it as against the outside public. That is his point.
And here is Hr. Courtney's reply to the taunt flung at him that the Cobden Club had abandoned the principles, and had gone in favour of protection by honouring the right hon. leader of this government by giving him a gold medal :
My right hon. friend has referred to the presentation by the Cobden Club of a gold medal to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, adding he was thus recognized by the highest authority as an eminent free trader. I am an honorary member of that club, but I have never been an ordinary member, and I have never associated myself with any of its actions; and when I read that a gold medal had been presented to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, I could not but think that the Cobden Club had committed a betise. Sir Wilfrid Laurier is a person of eminence and of great standing and a man who possesses line rhetorical powers; but whether he is a master of political economy or of the principles of free trade, I do not know. But I am certain that his action in proposing to reduce the duties on British produce imported into the Dominion of Canada was not of a character which should .have Recommended itself to Mr. Cobden. I think that he would not have accepted it. Mr. Cobden would have known a good deal better than that, and he Would have been the last to approve of it.
Now, the only argument of hon. gentlemen on the government side against the principles embodied in the second part of the resolutions at present before the House is that the English people will not entertain it, that the English people cannot do it. But these hon. gentlemen have never tried,

they have never made application to Great Britain for a preference. How is there to be a closer union between the different parts of the empire unless it is based upon the principle proposed by Hr. Chamberlain, the only principle he entertained-a zoll-verein of tariffs ? We must make the material interests of the mother country and of the colonies identical. Of course, we are not going to part with any portion of the right of self government, even to the Imperial authorities. We have the right to govern ourselves, as have other colonies of the empire. There is no proposition for Imperial federation or for closer union of interests as between the different parts of the empire, but the proposition of Mr. Chamberlain of a zollverein of tariffs between the different parts of the empire. That is the goal which the Conservative party are approaching. The right lion, leader of the government and the Minister of Finance, in discussing the subject the other day asked this side of the House :	If you are opposed to the preferential tariff, why do you not move to strike it out ? It never struck the hon. gentlemen that there was another way out of the difficulty. We can give protection against the manufactures of Great Britain coming into this country, and at the same time give preferential treatment to British goods. We do not abandon our protectionist principles, nor are we flying in the face of the preferential tariff. We can cany out the principle embodied in tbe second part of tbe resolutions without the abandonment of the preferential treatment of Great Britain. On the two parts of the resolution introduced by my hon. friend tbe leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), I am in complete accord with him; and I believe that the universal sentiment of the people of this country is in favour of carrying out the principle of political economy as laid down by all the great men of the present day, and in every civilized country of the world, with the single exception of Great Britain.
If at any time the industries and manufactures of the mother country were being swept out of existence by foreign competition, you would think she would protect her own industries. A few years ago she stood at the head of the manufacturing industries. She had cheap labour, skilled labour, any ^amount of capital for the purpose of distributing her products to every part of the world. If rival enterprises were started in any part of the world, she was able to send her goods into that country so cheap that she could undersell them and stifle their industries, and keep the market for herself. The ultimate goal of every country in this world, as plainly laid down by Mr. De Witte, is to have industrial and manufacturing centres surrounded by an agricultural population which will fur-
nisli the food products for the purpose of keeping up those industries. That doctrine is the fundamental doctrine of the Conservative platform. As I have already said, it may be that for a time the purchaser will suffer ; but the result is always beneficial ; and, as Mr. De Witte has pointed out, the people who adopt that policy always become the wealthiest and most intellectual.
Now, as to the remaining clause of the resolution introduced by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition :
The House is further of opinion that equivalent or adequate duties should be imposed by Canada upon the products and manufactures of countries not within the empire in all cases where, such countries fail to admit Canadian products and manufactures upon fair terms.
That opens a very wide field, it touches upon our relations with every other country in the world in respect of which Great Britain has bound us by the most-favoured-nation clause. It must apply to all, because no nation which has a most-favoured-nation clause with Great Britain could apply exceptional tariffs against this country, they would be void. They are similarly bound in their contracts with the empire to afford the same treatment to the colonies as to the empire. There are perhaps only three countries in the world to which we could apply that principle, namely, the zollverein of Germany, Belgium and the United States. Those treaties were denounced, and concerning the denunciation of those treaties I have some very interesting correspondence between the Colonial Secretary and the government of this country. It is in reference to the proposition that was introduced by the Finance Minister, offering most favourable terms not only to Great Britain but to any other country in the world that fulfilled the conditions. On this side of the House we pointed out the impossibility of anything of that kind being done. I remember the Minister of Marine and Fisheries getting up and, with that style of his which seemed to say that after he had opened his mouth nothing further could be said, he stated in the most positive manner that he had read carefully the most-favoured-nation clause of Great Britain, and that the argument of the opposition was groundless. I was wondering why the government dropped that particular clause in their tariff arrangements, and I find the reason in a despatch from the Colonial Office which completely upsets the ideas those gentlemen had when they first introduced their resolution, and brought them back to the position where they now stand :
But I should add that there is another question which is still more difficult, but about which I only wish to offer a word of warning to the representatives present. Besides these two treaties which are very special in their terms and which prevent the preferential arrangement, or which appear to prevent the preferential arrangement

Because the Colonial Secretary was very careful not to bind himself by saying that it did prevent the preferential arrangement; he wanted to leave a way of escape.
-we have a most-favoured-nation clause in all our treaties to which most of the colonies are I parties. I may explain that under the terms of the Canadian resolution, if any foreign nation were to offer to Canada beneficial terms as defined in the resolution, Canada would then be bound to give to that country the same preferences as offered to Great Britain. Let me suppose, for instance, that it was a minor country like Holland, and assuming for the sake of argument that Holland offered these conditions, thereupon Canada will be compelled to give the same terms to Holland that she now offers to the mother country. She would then be bound by the most-favoured-nation treaties to give the same terms to practically every commercial country in the world.
Repeating tbe words of the Colonial Secretary, nearly the ipsissima verba used by the leader of the opposition when he pointed out to the Finance Minister what would be the result of the proposition he made.
It would be, I think, a matter of impossibility to denounce those treaties because that involves the whole trade of the empire. In some cases there is no term of denunciation in the treaties. But, of course, the whole difficulty can be avoided by any colony which desires to make preferential arrangements with the mother country, if that colony will confine its offer nominatim to the mother country, and not make it to a foreign country.
That suggestion was made to the Finance Minister. He found out the solution of the difficulty that he was in, and that is the [DOT]cause of the change that he made in the resolutions after they were first introduced. But it never was the intention in this House, when those resolutions were introduced, to give virtually a 25 per cent tariff to the countries whose treaties we had denounced, to Germany, Belgium, and the rest of Europe. The result of the reduction in favour of Great Britain is virtually a reduction of nearly that amount in favour of the whole of Europe. Great Britain had practically the commerce of Europe at her disposition, and could carry her trade to all parts of the world, and could send even the products of Holland, Belgium, France and Germany into every part of the world.
What are these hon. gentlemen requiring under this preferential tariff ? Is it that 25 per cent of the original value of the article shall be finished in England ? I do not clearly understand the words of the order in council. I may be mistaken in that particular. Or, is it 25 per cent of the value of the article as it leaves the British shore? If it is the first proposition, suppose that an article costs $80 in Germany, and if 25 per cent of the finish is to be added in England, that would be only 20 per cent of the value of the article, and then you could add the cost of the package, the commission and

all these amounts to the value of the article sent to this country and you will find that the amount of the finish, or the expenditure to be made on the article in Great Britain, itself, will not amount to more than 20 per cent, or 15 per cent of the value of the article. That, as I understand it is the practice of the custom-house. Then, virtually, nearly every country in Europe is at the present time entering into competition with the manufacturers of this country on terms nearly equal to those accorded to the British people. That is what the people of this country will not permit. Germany has a hostile tariff against the people of this country, other countries have hostile tariffs against us, notably Germany, but, notwithstanding this fact, the policy which we adopted, not only in favour of the empire itself, but in favour of the different colonies, has been availed of to the fullest extent by Germany and there is an increased importation of German goods into this country under this preferential arrangement. What is the result of the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite ?-a prohibition, nearly, or at all events, a reduction to a large amount of the trade that we formerly did with the German people. Then, it is asked how the policy which we propose can he carried out. I heard the hon. Minister of Customs, the other day, ask the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean):	Would you
have a reciprocal arrangement with Great Britain ? Who ever contemplated such a thing ? There is no duty upon our goods going into that country and reciprocal treatment would he the taking off of the duty altogether on the goods coming into this country. We never contemplated any such absurdity as that, and the Conservative party have not fallen to such a depth of ignorance as to be propounding propositions the absurdity of which strikes the hon. Minister of Customs. What we propose to do is this: we know the difficulties In reference to the treaty arrangements by which we are bound to different countries in , the world. Surely we can make such a tariff arrangement as Germany and France have, that is. a maximum and a minimum tariff. Why should we not apply that principle to our own country ? It may be mechanical and self-working, so that, under certain circumstances and rules, as a result of the tariff which any country may adopt in reference to our trade, our tariff would go mechanically into force. That is one way of getting over the difficulties, and I would like the hon. Minister of Customs, when he is answering, to express his opinion in reference to it.
Would the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) answer one question ? When he says ' we ' does he mean himself, or does he mean the hon. member for East Tork (Mr. Maclean) ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF CUSTOMS (Hon. Wm. Paterson).

speechtext: I am speaking metaphorically for the people of this country. The Tooley street argument in reference to the tailors may apply, but it is the habit and custom of this House to speak of ' we,' and when I speak of ' we ' I speak as if I am here representing the people of tne country. I speak for my country and I am voicing the opinions of my country.

The impressions left on my mind by the speech of the hon. member for East York and the speech of the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) are entirely different, and, therefore, I wanted to know which view was the view of the party ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF CUSTOMS (Hon. Mr. Paterson).

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Paterson) makes a statement of fact which I controvert entirely. My views and the statement, as I heard it, of the hon. member for East York are quite consonant. He has an intelligent view of these matters and I, following in the wake of the hon. gentleman who spoke here the other day, am perhaps voicing in the concrete his opinions. These are the opinions that we hold in reference to this resolution. The hon. Minister of Customs, if he has any fault to find with them, or if he can find anything wrong with our principles, will be at liberty, in a short time, in discussing the matter, to show their fallacy, or falseness. Then, what is, after all, the resolution ? The resolution is an affirmation of tlie principles which, as I have said, since 1874 have bound the Conservative party. We state further that these principles have been departed from by tlie present government in order to make a revenue showing to the people, and that the present government are neglecting the manufacturing interests of the country. The right hon. gentleman (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier), in his argument, says that the people of this country' are sick of changes in the tariff. In order, under the protective system, to afford sufficient protection to- home industries, or to encourage the development of home industries, the tariff must of necessity be a changing one. Whenever we can manufacture articles cheaper in this country the tariff must be lowered a little to raise revenue and to afford competition which is a necessity in the interests of the manufacturers themselves. There is no fixed rate to be maintained. We will vary the tariff when we get in in order to carry out the system as we believe it should be carried out, to produce revenue in the country and to carry on, in accordance with the underlying principles of the Conservative party, the building up of the country, the building-up of industries which can be in no way done but by the adoption of the principles which this party have advocated from 1874, down to the present day. We further contend that the first duty of the people is to the country itself. For that reason we are
opposed to tlie one-sided arrangement which the right hon. gentleman made with the empire. There was no necessity for it. He, himself, made a statement before he went over to the old country entirely at variance with the policy which was adopted. His pre-election pledges to the people were in line with the second part of the resolution and the only way he gets out of his promise to the people is by presenting the argument, which was repeated by the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Russell), that the British government will not entertain a proposition of that kind and that no proposition of that kind will be entertained by any colony. They are making such propositions in Australia, and perhaps, before a couple of years have passed over the doctrine which the right hon. Secretary of State for the Colonies has laid down as the doctrine which will bind him in reference to the dealings between the different parts of the empire is that free trade principles shall not apply as between them. We have had statements made publicly in the House of Commons in England going to show that the Australian colonies are marching in that direction. Why is it that the man who made the nation, or woke up one morning and found that Canada was a nation, is not advancing the interests of the people by urging upon the Imperial government that free trade principles do not apply between the different parts of the empire and that they should ' give us something in return for our abandonment of the open door, and for our abandonment of every principle which the Cobden Club, and every free trader throughout the country has advocated for a number of years. I know that the conditions are altered, and that there is now no such limitations as there formerly was upon the assent to be given by the Governor General to tariff Bills. But, before that change was made, if you discriminated in favour of any country, the Bill would be retained, and you would not be allowed to do so. In some of the constitutions given to the different colonies, they are restricted in that sense. But, the information given to the people of this country through the Colonial Secretary was, that we should not discriminate even in favour of England. The Imperial government of the present day have abandoned that policy, and have come more than half way to meet the right hon. gentleman. Wliy is it he cannot see the signs of the times V Why is it he cannot see the Imperial spirit which pervades the empire from one end to the other, and which can only be voiced in a zollverein of tariffs, as Mr. Chamberlain says, because England will insist upon the freest government in her colonies, and the only advantage must be an Imperial one. they giving us a preference in their markets in return for the preference we are giving them. For these reasons. Mr. Speaker, I shall have great
pleasure in supporting the resolution which was introduced by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition.
