House in committee on Bill (No. 23) respecting the Guelph Junction Railway Company.-Mr. Guthrie.
On section 2,

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall this clause be adopted ?
No.
Yeas and nays.

I think that, perhaps, a little further explanation upon this clause might be well before we are asked to pass an opinion upon it There was not a very full meeting of the committee, so that the explanations which I made then may be quite new to many who are now present in the House. The Guelph Junction Railway is a road extending sixteen miles from the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway to the city of Guelph. Power is now asked to continue that road seventy miles further to Goderich. The road is practically the property of the city of Guelph. Its capital stock is $30,000. of which the city owns $20,000, fully paid up, the remaining $10,000 being in the hands of ten individuals, who are each entitled to $1,000, upon which each has paid 10 per cent, or $100. When the road was originally constructed in 1888, these ten men were active as directors. They were prominent business men and shippers in Guelph, all or nearly all large manufacturers, for whose benefit chiefly the road was built, because they wanted competition with the Grand Trunk Railway in freight rates. They were consequently the most active people in getting the road, and when the matter was submitted to the citizens, the citizens ratified it. When these men

tried to sell tlie bonds of the road, no one would buy them, and they were taken over by_ the city of Guelph, which invested $173,000 in them, making a total investment by the city, in bonds and stocks, of $193,000, whereas the private shareholders had invested only $1,000 in paid-up stock. These private shareholders have changed considerably since the road was constructed. Three of the most prominent are dead, and two of the shares are now held in the United States ; but the board has never changed. While the mayor of the city of Guelph, representing the $20,000 of stock, has the controlling vote for the board, he can only vote for five of these ten individuals who held the stock, as there were no other shareholders. The city of Guelph has taken the matter up. The board of trade of the city first passed upon it, then the city council passed upon it, both to the effect that the city should be given a larger selection-that as every ratepayer of Guelph was just as much interested in the road in reality as the stockholders, it would be reasonable to permit any bona fide ratepayer of the city of Guelph to be eligible as a director. A request was made before the Railway Committee that the Bill be amended in that way. Now, since the matter was first talked of in Guelph, the directors of the company have become active, and have complained that it is not fair to displace them now, after they have given their service freely for a number of years. That is true, but the service has been a very slight one, involving only the receiving of a cheque each year, and the handing of it over to the city. The road, as soon as it was constructed, was leased for 999 years to the Canadian Pacific Railway, the rental being 40 per cent of the gross earnings. Each year the Canadian Pacific Railway Company sends to the directors a cheque representing 40 per cent of the gross earnings, and the directors hand it over to the city. The bonds held by the city bear 5 per cent. The road has never paid any interest on the bonds, and there is a default in that respect amounting to about $10,000. If the city were disposed to be vindictive. it could apply to the courts and have a receiver appointed to collect this overdue interest but there is no intention of going to that extreme, and when this Bill to permit further time was coming before the House, the board of trade and the city council both thought that the cheapest and most expeditious way of obtaining the result would be to ask for the amendments which the Railway Committee have placed in the Bill. No real injury is being done to anybody ; no one is to be deprived of any property. The stock now held by the directors is to remain their stock ; they are still all to be eligible as directors ; but the anomaly of the present position is very apparent. By the original Act the city council is allowed three representatives on the Mr. GUTHRIE.
board, the mayor and two others ; the stockholders have five representatives on the board ; and the anomaly of the situation is that two-thirds of the stock has a minority on the board, and one-third of the stock, of which only 10 per cent has been paid, has a majority on the board. It would cure that anomaly to permit this amendment to pass. However, I understand that the city council would be quite willing to allow the stockholders a proportionate representation on the board, giving the city six representatives and the stockholders three. That would be a representation on the board according to the stock. All the city council desire is to appoint more active men as directors. If an amendment to that effect would be satisfactory, I think that would meet, probably, the views of both the citizens and the directors themselves, if their views are at all reasonable.
In that case, you had better move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Therefore, I would move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again.

Before the motion is put, I desire to say a few words on this Bill. The offer made by the promoter of the Bill may appear to be a very generous one ; but, to my mind, it will not lneet the views of the railway company which is interested, nor the views of the best business men of the city of Guelph. To give the directors only three on the board, while the city council has the privilege of naming six. of whom one will be the mayor, two aldermen, and the other three ordinary ratepayers. I do not think will be acceptable. The ratepayers selected by the mayor may be men of very small financial interest iii the city, and very little interest in the success of the road. The present mayor will not always be the mayor of the city of Guelph, and while the rights of the railway company may be safeguarded at the present time, there is no guarantee that the same safeguards would surround the future board. I look upon the treatment which these ten shareholders are to receive as altogether unprecedented in the history of legislation in this House.
Here are ten men who made themselves liable to the extent of $1,000 each, on the distinct understanding that they were not expected to pay more than $100 or 10 per cent on their stock. These men had given their services to the railway company, and practically to the city of Guelph, for some twelve or fifteen years. They have never exacted one cent as compensation ; they have given their services freely in the interests of the city and the people generally, and now this amendment seeks to place them in such a position that they will be
liable at once, if called upon by a majority of tbis board, for tbe full amount, and only three of them can now be on the board. Even if the amendment suggested by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) be carried, they will be entirely powerless to protect themselves, and will be liable for the entire amount of their stock, which it was distinctly understood they never should be called on to pay. That would leave them in a very unfair position, and unless the promoter of the Bill will grant these ten directors absolute relief from the payment of the remainder of their stock, as well as recoup them the amount of money they put into the railway with reasonable interest for the past ten years, I fail to see how this House can pass the proposed legislation. I trust the House will deal fairly with these ten enterprising men, leading citizens of Guelph. It is true that three of them have passed away, but one of them, the late J. D. Armstrong, well known to many members of this House, is succeeded by a young man of enterprise, ability and means, Mr. Lindsay Torrence, who represents his stock. Another succeeds his father-I refer to Col. Davidson of Guelph. So that there are not three men who can not act on the board. I believe that one of the shareholders sold the stock to a person who since moved to the United States, and I am also informed that it is his intention to get back the stock, so that as a matter of fact most of these enterprising business men of the city of Guelph are still shareholders of the company, and still available to be elected directors on this board. No better material could be found for a board than the very men who at present hold the stock of the company, and to displace these men, or displace even all but three of them, and place citizens upon the board, who may have no direct interest in the railway and little or none in tbe welfare of the city, is a step we should pause before taking. How are you going to expect men of enterprise and means to put their money into any investment in this country, if, after they have done so and rendered themselves liable for a considerable sum. this House is going to legislate away all the rights and safeguards with which they were surrounded and treat them in a way they never expected to be treated by the city of Guelph. I can scarcely believe that the citizens of Guelph, if their sentiments could be voiced to-night, would agree to the legislation proposed. Therefore, I cannot agree to the motion that the committee rise, with the intention of changing the directors so as to give the shareholders three seats on the board instead of the six they have now. I hold that until refunded their money and released from all liability, they ought to control the board.

It would be very unfair to pass this amendment, of which no notice has been given at all. The understanding was that these men, who took the risk, should control the board, and now it is proposed, without any notice, to make a change. If the city of Guelph thinks it in its interest to take over the road, these gentlemen should be first relieved of their liability and refunded the money they have paid with interest. I hope my hon. friend will not press this motion.

I am thoroughly in sympathy with the opposition to this motion. These directors paid 10 per cent each on their $1,000, and the understanding was that they should have one paid up share and be relieved from all further liability, but under this amendment they will be still liable for the balance of their stock. These men should be paid back their money with a reasonable amount of interest.

I *can hardly agree with my hon. friends who have spoken on the other side. As I understand it, this scheme was really a municipal one, one that was promoted and encouraged and all the expenses paid by the city of Guelph. It is true that some residents of the city, in whose interests, especially this scheme was being promoted, became shareholders and! paid into the treasury of the county $100 each.
And did the work.

No doubt they did a great deal of good work at the time, as was explained on a previous occasion. But many of these men have now passed away from this world, or for some other reason have lost all personal interest in this enterprise. Here is where I think a great injustice is done-these men contributed nothing except $100 each in connection with this matter ; but. as I understand it, the city of Guelph and the district are anxious that this railway should be extended ; and it may be quite possible that these men, not being represented on the board, may not have the same interest as the 'enterprising inhabitants of that city, or they may have some views with regard to this matter different from those of the people, and, by a majority vote, though they have but a small holding, they can override the wishes of the municipality which, as I understand it, holds a large majority of the stock in this enterprise and has contributed all the money to defray expenses. Any person with municipal experience knows that it is a common thing for men in large manufacturing or other businesses to contribute something in a small way, -as was done in this case, to some important enterprise. The hon. gentleman from Centre. Wellington (Mr. McGowan) refers to my hon. friend from South Wellington as pressing this matter. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Guthrie) is

simply acting upon a petition under the seal of the municipal council of the city of Guelph, expressing the wishes of the council, and, I suppose, of the people of the city. I quite agree with my hon. friend that it should be made clear that the gentlemen now living or their heirs, or assigns should be relieved of any future responsibility. I thought that was the understanding. And I believe my hon. friend from South Wellington is quite prepared to ask an amendment to this clause so that there can be no doubt about these persons being relieved of future liability on account of their subscription.

Will the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sutherland, Oxford) allow me a word ? I do not know much about this particular case, but a very simple way to achieve -what he speaks of would be for these gentlemen to transfer their stock to the city in consideration of the amount that has been paid upon it.

May I ask one question ? Why should a man who holds stock in a company be compelled to accept for it any amount that the city of Guelph may offer ? If he took it and became responsible for the balance, why should he be compelled to accept for it an amount fixed by another ? Take the case of the Bank of Montreal whose stock stands at $290 per share.
If I held a share of that stock for which I had paid $100, would it be fair to compel me to give it up on payment of $100 ? If we want to do that kind of thing in this case, there should be some way to assess the value, and, if you compel the holders to give up their shares, you should pay them what the shares are worth on the market to-day.

The hon. gentleman propounds a theoretical question, but I will tell him the exact state of affairs and will then ask him what he would do. He wants to know why a man should be forced to accept a low price for a valuable share. Of course, any legislation of that kind would be wrong. But, in this case, it is well known in this House or out of it that there is no value in these shares.
Mi'. GOURLEY. I do not know it. There is no evidence to that effect.

There is plenty of evidence to show that there is no value in this stock. But, even if there were value in it, why should a few men or their representatives be able to block the will of a municipality, and the surrounding district, by stopping a public enterprise ?
I do not know that that is the case there, but I do know that the representatives of the people have petitioned the government to grant this amendment and have given the reasons for it. I think we should be Mr. SUTHERLAND (Oxford).
perfectly right, even if the principle which the hon. gentleman states were being violated, if we provided that the municipality that granted this large bonus and held the principal amount of stock should be tree to carry out their enterprise in the direction indicated by the petition of the municipal council. As I understand it, a good many of these men are dead and the holdings have gone into the hands of other people. And if, owing to some arrangement made fifteen or twenty years ago, the enterprise has drifted into such an unfortunate position as indicated, it is the duty of parliament, on the petition of a municipality to place them in a position to get the benefit they should have.
What unfortunate position have they drifted into ? I am a member of the committee and I have heard nothing of it.
In such an unfortunate position that a small minority of the stock can control the whole-enterprise as against the vast majority of those interested as represented by the municipal council.
But they have done the business thoroughly well.

The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sutherland, Oxford) has not answered my point. Perhaps I did not state it cleanly. As I understand it, when the bargain was made and all these risks were taken, they were willing to trust these gentlemen to control the board. Now, they say -and this is why I cannot see my way- we want parliament to change that without recouping these gentlemen. I would be perfectly willing to carry out this, if that difficulty were removed

pay these gentlemen their $100 and interest and take over their stock.

As 1 understand it, my hon. friend from South Wellington was ready to move this subsection :
The directors of the said company may and shall, upon the request of the present shareholders of the company upon whose shares 10 per cent only have been paid, issue a fully paid-up share or shares to such person or persons in exchange for and to the extent of the aggregate amount paid by him or them upon his or their present shares.
That does not cover the other point.
It does not cover the $100. But my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) will see that there is nothing in that point, because the most of those for whom it is proposed are dead and gone.
No.

There are some who are alive. But I understand
that in the committee tihe statement was made and not disputed that many of them were dead and their stock assigned to those who did not take a personal interest in the enterprise. I am informed that three of the directors are dead and gone. One hon. gentleman suggested that there was no notice. I think parties interested had notice, for the simple reason that they were present here and were able to state their case before the committee. But the majority of the committee thought that the Bill should be reported in its present form.

I am sure there is no disposition on the part of this committee to take up a great deal of time on tills matter.
We are all interested in pushing the work as rapidly as we can, and I suggest that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again, and that then a motion be made that the Bill be referred back to the Railway Committee. It is clear that some new proposals are intended to be made, the hon. member who is moving in the matter desires to amend the Bill as it passed the Railway Committee. The terms of that amendment, before agreed upon, will likely require to be thoroughly looked into. I think the Railway Committee would be the proper place to do so ; it would facilitate 'matters to send it back there and let us have the question settled there. I second the motion of my hon. friend that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again, with the understanding that when the Speaker is in the Chair a motion may be made referring the whole matter back to the Railway Committee.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext:
I am willing to accept the proposition of the Minister of Railways, but I think it should be accompanied with a promise on the part of the promoter of the Bill, or a statement of how far he will go in the amendment which he is about to propose. If he will say to-night that he will submit an amendment authorizing the city of Guelph to pay these men back their hundred dollars and interest on the money from the time they invested it, and indemnify them against any further claim, I have no hesitation in saying that the Bill will go through ; but it is only on fair terms of that kind that I think this House should permit that Bill to go through. I believe that will be satisfactory to the railway company, they will then step out of the matter altogether, they will have no further liabilities, their money will be returned to them, and it will be to a certain extent a matter of fairness to all concerned. Now, with regard to that petition, I am going to venture a statement which came to me pretty directly, that even the city council of Guelph was taken by surprise when this petition was presented to the council and approved of ; that the members of the coun-01
cil were not aware that such a petition was coming before them, they had no notice of it, and they were rather taken by surprise. I say that subject to correcttion, but the information I have is obtained from one of the directors of this road, so that we should not lay too much stress on the fact that the city of Guelph had petitioned for this change. I am willing that the committee should rise, and give the hon. gentleman time to prepare his amendment, either in this committee or in the Railway Committee, perhaps better in the Railway Committee ; but I wish to say before doing so that I expect he will go as far as I have stated, that he will be willing that these men should be recouped their hundred dollars and interest, and be relieved from any further liability.

It would be difficult at present I think to come to any understanding as to the terms of settlement. The hon. gentleman would have to confer with these people. It must always be in the power of the Railway Committee to pass a Bill in such shape as will be found just and fair all round. We are not going to be precluded from freedom of action in the Railway Committee by consents which may be arrived at. Let us see that justice is done in the legislation.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think we should go further than that. Before we refer this Bill back we ought to see that certain instructions accompany it to the Railway Committee to amend it in that direction.
We do not know what we will decide upon in the Railway Committee.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Then I want to say a word with regard to this Bill.
My suggestion was to save time.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: When the Bill is referred back with the understanding or instructions that it is done for a certain purpose, it would be easier to change it in the Railway Committee. In the first place, this Bill proposes what we have never done before, that is to allow the appointment of a director that is not worth a dollar. The Railway Act provides what is the qualification of a director. He shall own so much stock, he shall have an interest in the road, so that he shall be something more than a man of straw. But this amendment provides that a man may be appointed a director who is only a tool or a catspaw of the mayor : he may not be worth a dollar, and not a dollar's worth of property in the world, so long as he is a citizen of Guelph. That looks suspicious on the face of it.
He may be entitled to represent the town in its minor interests.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There is no provision that a director should be worth a dollar.
He is qualified to be an aider-man.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
There is no qualification in this amendment for a director. The Railway Act provides that no person shall be a director unless he is a shareholder holding stock absolutely in his own right and qualified to vote for directors at the election at which he is chosen. But this does not provide that he shall own a dollar's worth of stock ; but any one may be picked up off the street to suit the mayor's purpose. Now, it must not be forgotten that the parties who are being crowded off the board to-day are the parties that took hold of the scheme when it was of no value, either to the corporation or to anybody else, they are the parties who engineered it, and financed it, and built the railway and gave the city of Guelph all the advantages it is receiving from the railway to-day. The parties who now desire this scheme were quite content to let the company go on and do the work and raise the money when it seemed to be impossible to raise the money to build a railway. But they succeeded in doing that, and putting it on a good financial basis, until the railway is a paying concern to-day, and now' an effort is being made to force these men out wrho paid up all that was necessary for their stock, to force them out without giving them a cent for that stock or relieving them from the liabilities which they are under to pay the balance of that stock if they are called on. Now. the proposal made by Colonel McRae, I think, was a reasonable one. He said : If these parties want to get our stock, let them pay us back our money, take the stock from us and release us from any further liability. But they did not choose to do that ; and will this House pass a law to compel men to abandon their rights and to give up their property without any consideration after they have made it valuable, when they are the only parties that have made a reasonable endeavour to give the city of Guelph the advantages of a railway that to-day is on a workable basis ?
Progress reported.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS moved that the said Bill be referred back to the Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines.
That can only be done at this stage w'ith the unanimous consent of the House.
I dissent.

['order to encourage the beet-root sugar industry and so to benefit the farmers, the government have decided, as the only change that they will make in the tariff since 1897, that they will allow machinery to come in free for the period of one year. I congratulate, as congratulations are the order of the day, the farmers upon the magnificent treatment they have received from the present administration.
Now, I want to refer to some of the hon. gentlemen who have spoken, but, as the hour is getting late, and as these hon. gentlemen have all absented themselves, I am not going into it as extensively as I intended to. The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), who is a very eloquent speaker, made some remarks that I think deserves a passing reference. He compared the resolutions brought in by the Conservative opposition to ' the emergency rations.' I want to tell that hon. gentleman, and I want to tell those who cheered the allusion, that whatever divergence of opinion we may have as regards the difficulty that arose over the emergency rations to South Africa, it does not come well from that side of the House to refer to that question in this way. I cannot say whether, in the inception of that matter the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence was to blame. That is a debatable question. But, I am here to say, and I say it with a feeling ol' the full responsibility, that the government cannot be acquitted of blame in this, that when the difficulty had been shown to them, when the wrong had been shown to have been perpetrated, when it had been shown that a crime, than which it would be difficult to find one more dastardly, had been committed with reference to our brave soldier boys in South Africa, there was a duty cast upon the government and that duty has not been discharged. Therefore, I say, it does not become the hon. member for South Wellington or "any other hon. gentleman on that side of the House to say any more about emergency rations than they cau help. Now, these hon. gentlemen differ so much amongst themselves as to what the policy of the government is that it is probably better to let them fight it out amongst themselves. For instance, the hon. member for South Wellington is in favour of bounties, and there is no more definite or distinct system of protection than bounties. 1-Ie says he is for bounties up to the hilt. Then he proceeds to struggle with the questions of the surplus and to point out, or to try to show, that a surplus is not inconsistent with a policy of 1 a tariff for revenue only.' He struggled with a ghost, because there is no surplus and he met ghosts because the ghost of the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) and the ghosts of many other hon. members confronted him in that regard. I will read just a line in reference to the question of bounties from a statement by
the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Sir Louis Davies). He was making a tour of the maritime provinces and say in regard to bounties :
This country cannot he made poor; it must continue in wealth and prosperity. But he was not satisfied to be contented with a mere existence, but desired to see Canada take the fullest advantage of its great resources. This could only be accomplished in one way, by means of free trade. This was the key with which they would unlock the golden door of prosperity. . . The Liberals maintained that any trade which required subventions to keep them alive, not only do not contribute to the natural wealth, but actually hinder the prosperity of a country. This is pretty clear upon the question of bounties. I leave my hon. friend from South Wellington to tight it out with the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, although perhaps, it may very well be that the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries has varied his opinion very much since that time. We had a very eloquent speech from the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil), and I must say that after the eloquent manner in which he seconded the address it was unfortunate indeed that he should be the first, and I am glad to say, the only hon. gentleman,who introduced the race and religious cry in this House. I followed the hon. gentleman through his somewhat labourious argument designed to show that certain constituencies in Quebec with an admittedly Roman Catholic majority had sent hon. gentlemen of another religion to represent them on the floor of this House. X did not know until then, living in the province of Ontario, and I regret it if it obtains in Quebec, that these questions are taken into account in the matter of elections. I have always found, in the province in which 1 live, that whatever a man's religion may be, or whatever his nationality may be, it cuts no figure in the question as to whether he should or should not represent a certain electorate in the Dominion, or any legislature, and I regret exceedingly to find that we should have an argument to show that in any province of this country, or in any part of this country, another state of things prevails.
We had a speech from the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Roche) which certainly had no very direct bearing on the question before the House. It was a speech which should not be lost sight of, because it was unique. The hon. gentleman congratulated us on this side upon the research and deep study which we have evidently given to the financial questions which are being discussed. I can endorse his remark there. We on this side of the House have brought to the consideration of public questions an honest determination to sift them to the bottom, to get facts and figures to support our arguments, and to submit them in a fair and honourable way. Having paid us this compliment, it 62
would seem that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche) must have dived into the coal mines of his imagination, because he brought up a considerable amount of that material by which he tried to blacken the position taken by hon. members on this side. However, we must to some extent forgive him for he concluded by whitewashing us again. The hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) stated that the third paragraph of the resolution introduced by the hon. leader of the Conservative party (Mr. Borden), is a distinct declaration of a tariff war against the world. Do hon. gentlemen upon the other side of the House concur in that statement ? Surely any one who brings a fair mind to bear upon the question must recognize that the principle we enunciate is that we shall expect the same treatment from other nations that we are prepared to extend to them. There is no declaration of war there. Did not the hon. gentleman from Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), when he spoke on Mr. Bennett's motion, tell us that if we wanted to be respected by the people of the United States we must assert our rights and show that we are ready to maintain them. That is the principle of the amendment which the Conservative party have enunciated in parliament, and that is the principle which the people of Canada are prepared to maintain.
I had not the pleasure of hearing the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright), although he is the gentleman above all others whom I particularly desired to hear, because I believed it would be more difficult for that gentleman than for any other to deal with these financial questions. He is upon record on all the questions that enter into this discussion. Beginning his life with associations better than the associations which surround him now, beginning his life as a staunch Conservative, and having the variegated history that he has had since, if there is a pathetic picture upon the floor of the House of Commons to-day it is the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Trace him through the unfortunate circumstances which have compelled him to take the position he now occupies. See him leave the old Conservative party without a cause. See him next, as he was represented here the other evening, a believer in protection, but an enforced advocate of free trade. See him go through this country from one end to the other denouncing the policy that he loved and upholding the policy of free trade which was perforce to be his road to the portfolio of finance. And in the end see that hon. gentleman (Sir Richard Cartwright) whom I certainly very much admire ; see him in the end landed not in the position he naturally expected, but stranded and relegated to a position which he did not covet. He has told more than one audience in this eoun-', "

try exactly what he thinks of his present portfolio of Trade and Commerce. He has told them that it is a perfectly useless portfolio, that it should never have been created, that it is a department in which a man cannot earn one dollar of the salary which is paid him. See him occupying that position now, compelled, reluctantly, I hope to draw the emolument which is attached to that office, and no matter what our political opinions may be, it must be a pathetic picture to us to see him as he is. It is pathetic to see him obliged to stand up and state that the expenditure of this government is right, that the policy of this government is a free trade policy, in a word swallowing all that he has said, feeding as he does on husks ; feeding on the light literature he has spread broadcast through this country in his various speeches, and swallowing his record whole. I sincerely sympathize with the hon. gentleman. Mr. Speaker, I must apologize to the House-but the apology will only extend to a small portion of it in view of the emptiness of the Liberal benches. I do feel as a new member that though I have had a splendid subject and a magnificent opportunity, I have not availed myself of it, not from want or will, but because of want of ability to deal with these questions as efficiently as I would desire. In conclusion let me point to what I think is a fortunate thing in the midst of that which to some extent is a misfortune. I recognize that it is a very serious misfortune for this country that by a side issue, and by nothing else, that by a side issue and by a fluke this government came into power. But, while it is a great misfortune, a misfortune which I believe the people of this country recognize to-day, there is one thing upon which we should congratulate ourselves, and this is that we have just come to that stage in our political history when the people of Canada know exactly where we stand. For eighteen years, while the Conservatives were in pow-er, and while the Conservative policy was calculated to work great good for Canada, there was still the great disadvantage that the members of the Liberal party, great and small, went up and down the country decrying our policy and thereby preventing it from having that full beneficial effect that it otherwise would. But that is not all. They not only did that, but by telling the people -and there were some people foolish enough to believe them sincere- that they were coming into power, and that when they came into power they would remove every vestige of protection and revert to the old free trade, which had ruined this country before. By doing so they retarded the prosperity of the country and prevented the building up of its industries to the extent to which they would otherwise have been built up under the Conservative policy. They told the people that they were Mr. LENNOX.
coming into power, and would put into force one or other of the five or six policies which they had propounded, and that protection would be set aside. As me Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher) said so eloquently on many occasions-referring to the Conservative policy of protection-this accursed system, a system accursed by God and man, and it was going to be wiped out.' So that people stood hesitating and doubting, and doubt means distrust, <md distrust in commercial matters means ultimate bankruptcy. While a great many people did not believe them, yet it did, to a certain extent, retard the onward march of the national policy during those eighteen years. But, when they came into power, it was found that they had not the courage to inaugurate any of the policies they had been preaching. I ask the hon. members of the government, will they tell me which of the policies they advocated they have adopted ? Is it continental free trade V I know they will say it is not. Is it commercial union with the United States ? I know they will say it is not. Is it unrestricted reciprocity ? I know they will say it is not. Is it free trade? That is the only one they can escape on. They will not say that it is. Is it a tariff for revenue only ? The Minister of Finance came down here the other day and said this : A year ago I told the people of this country that we would reach the fifty-million mark in revenue. The revenue required is for an expenditure of $42,000,000. On a tariff for revenue only the hon. gentleman takes from the pockets of the people of this country $8,000,000 in excess of what he says is required for the expenditure of the country. How can he say, under these circumstances, that it is a tariff for revenue only ? Is it free trade as they have it in England ? No. And so it comes to this, that take it whatever way you will, these hon. gentlemen were never able, during the eighteen years that they were out of power, to devise a policy which was workable in the interest of this Dominion ; and when they came into power they were in this position, that they had to send a commission out to try by questions, such as they fling across the House to try to draw our hands, to devise a policy which they were not able to devise for themselves. The result was that when they got the report of that commission, they had to adopt in effect the old policy of the Conservative party, and they have attached to it a clause with reference to preferential trade, which has had no effect except to make it more difficult for the industries of this country to prosper. In the cotton industry alone we find that the stock has dropped to-day seventeen points. So that the result which is going to follow from this preferential tariff is making its appearance already.
I feel that I have already spoken longer than probably I ought as a new member ; but you will recognize that it is much more

difficult for us new members to speak than the old and hardened gentlemen who sit on the other side of the House, yes and some of whom sit on this side, but to our left. I would not for a moment say anything disrespectful of the members of the government. I think the time has come when we have it, as a firmly established idea, that protection shall be the main policy of this country. Good men are wanted now, and this is about all we want to have assured prosperity in this country. I say nothing disrespectful of the administration of this country, only I think they could be improved upon, some of them perhaps a great deal. I was walking the other day along Sparks street, when I saw an advertisement in a window. If 1 had consulted my own feelings vipon this occasion, I may say that I would have retained my seat, but, as a resolution is before the House, as an amendment lias been moved and as a debate has taken place which has brought up certain questions of supreme importance, not only to the county which I have the honour to represent, but also to the province of Nova Scotia, as well as to the rest of the Dominion, I feel that 1 would not be properly discharging my duty did 1 not rise to say a few words. It. is not my intention to delay the House for any great length of time. My purpose in rising is to address myself exclusively to two or three subjects which have been presented to our consideration during the course of the debate. The question which is raised by the first clause ot the amendment of the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) is the old question of protection, the old question of the national policy. That national policy was before the people for a number of years, it was tried, it was weighed in the balance, it was found wanting and the people pronounced against it upon two separate occasions with no uncertain voice. The tariff which was framed after that by the present hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) has been before the people and has been endorsed by such an overwhelming majority of the electors as should satisfy that hon. gentleman. It was said, however, after the introduction of the tariff of 1897, that the people had been deceived by the Liberal party, that they went to the country in 1896, not upon the tariff which was framed by the hon. Minister of Finance, but on a free trade tariff as opposed to protection. Now, it does seem strange to me that hon. gentlemen will, at this late day, repeat that contention when it has been falsified over and over again. Every one knows-and there cannot be found an utterance of a solitary man who stood in the position of a leader of the Liberal party to the contrary-every one knows that the tariff which the Liberal party promised previously to 1896 was a revenue tariff, or as we call it a free trade revenue tariff, as opposed to the protective revenue tariff which was in force under Mr. SPROULE.

Conservative rule. The distinction between these two tariffs is so evident, that I feel like apologizing for referring to it on this occasion. The Conservative tariff was designed for the purpose of protecting certain selected industries, whether it protected the other industries or not. It has been stated in this House that the Conservative tariff protected the manufacturers, but that it did not protect the natural industries of the country, and revenue was only an incident of that tariff. Now, the Liberal tariff is exactly the reverse of that. It is framed for the purpose of producing revenue, and if it incidentally gives protection to certain industries so much the better. That is the distinction between the two tariffs. We stood by this tariff, and on it we went to the country. But, as I have said, our opponents in the last election went before the people and told them they had been deceived by us. Our opponents said-it was pretty hard to follow their meaning too- they said in the first place to us : You promised the people free trade and you did not give them free trade; what you did give them is our old national policy. Well, we felt like saying to these gentlemen:	If we
have given the country your old national policy, what are you growling about, you should be satisfied; if we have put on your garments you should feel flattered, but you certainly have nothing to complain of; if we have made these promises the only people who can complain are the people we made them to and surely you should be the last to complain because you always said that you never would believe a word we uttered or credit a promise we made.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I submit that we made no promise of free trade, but that the promise we did make was simply the promise of a revenue tariff. When this tariff whicli was introduced by the Finance Minister (Hon. Mr. Fielding) in 1897. was placed before the House, the first authoritative utterance we had upon it from the Conservative ranks was the speech made by the then leader of the opposition (Sir Charles Tupper). It is a very lengthy speech. I have read it all with great care as it appears in ' Hansard,' and I shall quote one passage from it to show what Sir Charles Tupper's idea was of the Liberal tariff introduced in 1897. He said :
The result is that this tariff goes into operation, and the hon. gentleman (referring to the Hon. Mr. Fielding) knows that the industries of this country are already paralyzed in consequence, while hon. members opposite gloat over the destruction of Canadian industries. I was reading the wail, the sorrowful wail, of those industries in the Montreal Gazette, where one manufacturer after another declared that those industries were ruined, that their mills must close, and that they saw staring them in the face a return to the deplorable state of things that existed when the hon. gentleman who last addressed the House, was in charge of the fiscal policy of the country. I say that a deeper wrong was never inflicted upon Canada.
That was the first utterance from the Conservative party with reference to the tariff of the Liberal government. Well, the wail did not materialize. The industries of Canada were not destroyed. On the contrary, tlie country became very prosperous under this new tariff, and the hon. gentleman (Sir Charles Tupper) who was responsible for the words I have quoted attempted on various occasions afterwards to explain away how he came to make that statement. He and Ills friends said that the tariff was altered after the speech was made. It is true that the tariff was altered slightly. There were some necessary changes in the tariff the total effect of which upon the whole revenue collected during the next year was less than half a million dollars, and the hon. gentleman (Sir Charles Tupper) and his friends told us that was the excuse for saying :	1 Oh, this tariff as introduced was
a thing that was going to destroy all the industries of the country, but with these slight changes it becomes the old national policy.' Now, Sir, I wish to assert in this House, and I think I have evidence before me to bear out the assertion, that the people of Canada previously to the election of 1896, were displeased and dissatisfied with this national policy. It was a disappointment to them. I do not know that I can prove this In any better way than by quoting the words of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell). Every one knows that he had been a strong admirer and supporter of the national policy, but he in common with thousands of others throughout the Dominion became disappointed and discouraged and disgusted, and in 1891, Mr. Bell delivered a most excellent lecture I am told in the city of New Glasgow where he resides, and he spoke these very forcible words on that occasion-because he is always forcible in his language as we all know. He said :
I consider the argument of the free trade as unanswerable. I believe that this moment if Canada took a liberal step in the direction of free trade it would go a long way to place her upon the road to the greatest prosperity.
Now, that has the true ring about it. Well, Canada did take a step in that direction. We are told by the Finance Minister (Hon. Mr. Fielding) that the effect of the tariff he introduced has been to reduce the taxes that would have been collected under the Conservative tariff by one-eighth or by about 12i per cent. But the hon. gentleman from Pictou (Mr. Bell) on that occasion proceeded [DOT]to give his reasons for the faith that was in him and his reasons were, most cogent, and they were reasons which must carry a great deal of weight. He said :
The reasons why I consider Canada should turn about and adopt a free trade policy are :
(a)	that we might free ourselves of the dominating influence of the United States.
But, to-day my hon. friend (Mr. Bell) tells us that the only way by which we can free ourselves from the dominating influence of


the United States is by adopting protection; protection pure and simple. The question therefore is: whether he was right in 1891, or whether he is right in this present year, ten years afterwards. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bell) gives another reason. He says :
(b)	On account of the failure of the national policy.
Mow, Mr. Speaker, that is a terrible heresy coming from the gentleman who stood up here the other night to laud and defend the national policy.
(c)	Because of the startling revelations of the census.
You see, Mr. Speaker, he voices the very arguments that we Liberals made use of, and he gives the very reasons that we assigned. We said the national policy was a disappointment ; we said the country did not prosper under it; we said the population had not increased as it should have increased, and we said that the national policy was not doing anything to remove us from the dominating influence of the United States. And so the hon. gentleman (Mr. Belli was on our side of the argument in 1S91, and I only quote his words as an authority for saying that there was dissatisfaction in 1896 against the protective tariff policy, or the national policy as it was styled.
But there was a new feature introduced in the tariff proposed by the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) in 1897. You know, Sir, that during all these years in which we wandered in the wilderness of opposition the Conservatives monopolized almost entirely the loyalty of all Canada. They appropriated the old flag and they would scarcely allow us to have a bit of it. They were very loyal in speech, but they never had done anything to prove their loyalty. But, when the Finance Minister brought down this preferential feature of his tariff by which he allowed goods from the mother country to be brought in at a lower rate of duty than goods from other countries which did not treat us as the mother land did, what did these hon. gentlemen opposite say ? In the first place their statement was : Oh, you have made a vast mistake, you never can work this out because of the German and Belgian treaties. In the next place, they said it would amount to nothing anyhow; it made no difference. Well, this Belgian and German treaty bugbear was removed, and ultimately they had to face the situation; ultimately they had to take a stand and say whether they were in favour of this preference to the mother country or not. They were driven to that; and what position did they assume ? They assumed the position of talking against it, but they never challenged it by a vote or a motion, and I doubt if they will do so, no matter how valiantly they may talk.
Now, I submit to all reasonable parties, that the granting of a preference to the

mother country was a most wise step. I believe that plank in the platform of the Liberal party contributed most largely to the success of the Liberal party in the last election ; and for this reason. I believe there is abroad throughout the Dominion of Canada a sentiment of attachment to the empire, and I believe this-and I would be ashamed to believe anything different- that there exists in the breast of every honest Canadian, no matter what his race may be, a sense of gratitude towards the mother country for what she is doing for us. We are living here to-day under the protection of the British flag ; we have British guns at Esquimalt and at Halifax ; we have the British navy ready to defend us on all occasions ; we have the full use of British diplomacy and the British consular corps all over the world, so that no matter how humble the Canadian may be, no matter in what part of the world he may be found, if the government of the country in which he finds himself does not do him ample justice, or if it inflicts an injury upon him, the whole force and power of the British Empire is brought to bear to defend him. And who has paid for all this ? The British taxpayer. Have we ever paid one dollar ? Have we ever been asked to contribute one cent ? Never. And yet, Sir, when we have given to the mother country simply this reduction in the tariff which we raise against other nations which have tariffs against us, we are condemned. All our manufactures, all our foodstuffs, everything we have to sell in the markets of the world, are admitted into Great Britain free of duty. But when England sends her wares to us, we meet them with a tariff, and we have been condemned solely because we have given her a preference. Do any of these gentlemen ever pause to consider what would be the effect upon Canada if England treated us exactly as we treat her -if she raised the same tariff wall against us that we have against her ? It seems to me that some of the gentlemen who have spoken with regard to the industries of Canada have not paid any attention to that part of the question.

That in the opinion of this House the welfare of this country requires a pronounced policy of adequate protection and encouragement at all times to the labour, agricultural, manufacturing, mining and other industries of Canada.
I have listened for days with the greatest attention to' almost everything that has fallen from the lips of hon. gentlemen opposite ; I have read, I think, most that has been said by the leading men on that side since the inauguration of the national policy ; and I have yet to discover where

Now, there is just one other matter I wish to refer to and that is the question of railway subsidies, because it is interwoven with this question of free transportation, as I have stated. The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) solemnly declared- forcmiy declared I should say-on behalf of the opposition, I assume, for he was sitting- next to the leader of the opposition at the time, and that lion, gentleman seemed to be well pleased with his remarks and, though he and other lion, gentlemen have spoken since then, not a word of discredit has been thrown on his utterance, that it was time for the government to call a halt. It makes the hon. senior member for Pictou (Sir Charles Hib-bert Tupper) smile. I do not wonder, when the hon. member for West Toronto was the one put up to say that thing. In Nova Scotia we commenced early to agitate for railways-away back in the fifties. If my memory serves me right the first legislation in that direction was passed in 1854. It was the policy of the government in that day to build and own the railway. In this they were strongly denounced by the opposition. But they went on with their scheme and, in 1858 they had a railway completed and in operation from Halifax to Truro and from Halifax to Windsor. And, when the government railway building was interrupted by confederation in 1867, we had completed the line from Truro to Pictou; and I have not the slightest doubt that had we not gone into confederation, the government policy would have been pursued, and every part of Nova Scotia, which, to-day is clamouring for railway communication would have had it years ago. But we came into confederation, and. necessarily, a different policy was adopted.
Why did not you secede with the Finance Minister ?
We might have done so if we had not got the railway extended into Cape Breton.
The Finance Minister does not seem to have seceded very materially.

The complaint that was made the other night by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) was that the Finance Minister is a gentleman who sticks to office, and I believe he does. He is not a seceder. When the hon. gentleman opposite talks about secession, I think he is ill advised on the subject. If he had been down in Nova Scotia and heard the discussion that took place on the question of secession, or rather on tile question of better terms and the question of revising the union, he would be in a better position to talk upon the subject than he is now. If he wishes to know what the Nova Scotians said on that occasion, I do not hesitate to tell him, but that is beside my argument now.
When we entered confederation we had a certain quantity of railway built. The policy of the government was to keep on building railways, and I believe that if they had not been interrupted we would have had all the railroads we are now clamouring for. After we entered confederation a bargain was made with British Columbia by which this country undertook tlie burden of building the Canadian Pacific Railway. Then another condition of affairs existed, and we had to wait and take bur chances to get our roads built. We are not complaining of that. I am not complaining to-night because the Canadian Pacific Railway was built, I am not complaining because we had to wait to get our roads. What I am complaining of is that after we have waited for roads which are in the interest of the country and should have been built long ago, we should now be met with the statement that there should be no more subsidies granted to railways, and that from a gentleman coming from the place he does, and representing the company he does. Now, let us inquire for a moment what has been expended on works of this description. I find that since confederation we have given in cash bonuses the sum of $48,130,000, in addition to some other things. We have given 39.725,000 acres of land for railroads, that is outside of the Intercolonial Railway. On canals there was spent before confederation over $20,000,000, and since confederation we have spent over $58,000,000. The construction of the Intercolonial Railway, including the purchase of the Drummond County Railway, has cost the country upward of $60,000,000. In addition to that, we have expended immense sums upon river and harbour improvements and upon canal improvements in order to build up the country and make it more prosperous. I was pleased the other night to hear the Minister of Public Works declare that he was going on with this policy of public improvements. I submit that it is the duty of the government to go on. They can get cheap money, they can get money today for a trifle over 2i per cent interest,
where a private individual has to pay double that amount. Then is it not their duty to go on with these public works until every want of the country is satisfied ? Is not this a fair proposition, that a section of country which to-day demands and requires a railway, fifteen years ago did not require it ? And would it be honest or fair towards those sections which have contributed towards opening up other sections of country by railways, to be told now : We are going to call a halt, we are going to give no more subsidies to railways, we are going to have no more public works. We have gone far enough in our public works, we have * our railways constructed, now we are satisfied, and you have got to be satisfied. Now, where does this statement come from ? It comes from the province of Ontario, a province which is grid-ironed with Government aided railways. It comes from a province where the bulk of the money for canals has been expended ; it comes from the city of Toronto which has been made what it is by these great transportation systems which have been brought into existence by the liberal use of public money ; it comes from a director of the Canadian Pacific Railway, nearly every spike of which has been paid for by the Dominion of Canada. That is the position.
Now, I protest against that, I protest against it in the interest of the province that I come from, I protest against that policy in the interests of the county that I represent. The people of Annapolis county are clamouring for the construction of a railway from Victoria Beach to meet the Central, to connect with the Dominion and Atlantic Railway at Middleton. The people on the south shore of Nova Scotia are clamouring for a railway to be finished from Halifax to Yarmouth. A portion of that subsidy has been granted to the shore road, a portion of the subsidy has been granted by this government to the Victoria Beach road as far as Bridgetown and it only requires the granting of the additional subsidy upon the remaining 14 miles between Bridgetown and Middleton. Now, some hon. gentlemen, when I mentioned the South Shore road, said, hear, hear. Am I to understand that there are gentlemen opposite who claim that the South Shore road should be subsidized and completed ?
Yes.
Well, I am glad to hear him say so, I am glad he has got the courage of his convictions. But what does the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Kaul-bach) say ?
He will say the same.
We want 2,000 miles of railway in Nova Scotia the next two years.

be answered later on by an bon. gentleman who is to speak. I merely say in passing that I do not understand that the prefer-tial tariff gives cheaper goods to tjuuada, and I pass to an argument which has not been much made use of.
Members of the cabinet nave asserted in this debate that it is impossible to secure a fair trade with Britain on any other terms than the terms they have-in other words, that mutual concessions between Britain and Canada are absolutely impossible. But, let us remember that the gentlemen who are saying this are led by the right lion. First Minister, who when he went to Britain gave away all we had to give ; and it is not until after he has done this and had said ' Canada wants nothing in return,' that they come and tell us that the grand advantage which would result from an arrangement of mutual trade preferences between Britain and all her colonies cannot possibly be obtained. This is of a piece with the action of these gentlemen in other commercial matters. It is of a piece with their action on the Joint High Commission which went to Washington. Now, the resolution before the House has been read more than once. I want to ask the members of the government and their supporters : Do you object to the whole of it ? If not, what part of it do you object to ? We ask for adequate protection and encouragement to the agricultural, manufacturing and other interests of the country. Do hon. gentlemen object to this ? If they do, we want them to put themselves plainly upon record in that regard, because the people of Canada want to know just where they stand. Then, the resolution says that the time has come when, in the opinion of this House, the adoption of a policy of mutual trade preferences within the empire would prove of great benefit. Do the hon. gentlemen object to this ? If they do not, we will expect them to vote for it. Again it is said that the time is opportune. Is there a doubt about that ? It is opportune, not only in view of the inauguration of the Australian commonwealth, but also because the policy upon which the rebellious states in South Africa are to be governed has not yet been settled. There is going to be an enormous trade in that part of the world. It is important that Canada should secure a measure, and a large measure, of that trade. It is within the competence of Great Britain, without disturbing her present fiscal policy at all, to give us a preference in these markets, and, therefore, emphatically, taking into account the situation in Australia and South Africa, this is a most opportune time for a movement in this direction.
Do hon. gentlemen opposite claim that they have reverted to the policy which obtained prior to 1878, when the Mackenzie administration was in power. I do not think that any of them will be quite daring enough to do that. The disastrous and ruinous conditions which then prevailed were so startling that it would be dangerous for these hon. gentlemen to announce that they had reverted to the policy of those days, which was a policy of tariff for revenue only. At that time our trade fell steadily, year by year, from $210,000,000 to $170,000,000 or an average of $30,000,000 a year, or 14 per cent during every year the reform party was in power. What is required now is not a one-sided preferential tariff, but a firm, well defined, protective policy, whicli will develop, upon the old lines, the various industrial interests of this country.
Let me read you a few figures which will dispose of the claim of hon. gentlemen opposite that the preferential tariff has been the means of increasing the trade of Canada with Great Britain. In 1897 our aggregate trade with Great Britain was $100,000,000 in round numbers. In 1900, it had increased to $152,000,000, or a gain of 43'21 per cent. That, you will say, was a substantial gain, and I began with 1S97, because that was the year in which the government announced its policy. Until then they were hedging, ana inquiring, and issuing commissions. Well, our trade with Great Britain increased 43 per cent in that period, but let us see how that increase compares with the increase in the aggregate trade of Canada with the whole world. If we find that the trade with Great Britain advanced much more rapidly than our trade with the rest of the world, then of course that would be an argument in favour of the preferential rate, but the facts show that from 1897 to 1900, our trade with the rest of the world shows an increase, not of 43 per cent, but of 49 per cent. So that although we did a fairly good trade with Great Britain, it did not keep pace with our trade with the rest of the world.
Then, how does our trade with Great Britain compare with our trade with other countries ? We have no preferential tariff with Germany, at least no direct preferential tariff. But, we have an indirect and unjust preferential tariff with that country, by way of England, and also with a great many other foreign countries, who send their goods to England, whence they are shipped to us and get the advantage of the rebate. Well, our trade with Germany from 1897 to 1900 increased 33 per cent. Our trade with the United States, with which we have no preferential tariff, increased from 1897 to 1900, not 43 per cent, but 60 74 per cent-an increase far greater than that with Great Britain. try have come to the position where they demand aid will have a straight statement of t'leir affairs, such a straight statement as a business man would give. But the encouragement of labour too is one of those matters which might well form the subject of discussion in a budget speech, and I venture to say that if the Minister of Finance had had the courage to tackle the question he would have dealt with it. But, there is one great question which is going to require more thought at the hands of the honest representatives of the people of this country in the near future than any other, and that is, the best way of bringing to market the great resources of this country from the west. A comprehensive policy upon this question is what the people require, and what an administration that is powerful enough and wise enough should outline at this time. Bead the budget speech from end to end, and where do you get one idea, one indication of what the policy of this government is to be as regards the carrying trade ? We are developing mines, the products of which have helped to swell the coffers of the Dominion treasury. But, although this is the case, and although the farmers are putting forth every effort to develop new lines of industry, and looking to the best means of getting their produce to the markets of the world, the administration seem to have given the subject no attention.
Where a multiplicity of routes is suggested and with routes in almost every direction, with railway -schemes looming up from almost every township, it is of the utmost importance that we should give our attention to this question and it was the duty of the government to consider this question well so as to be able to outline a plan clearly before the people, in order that those who want to invest money in future in commercial enterprises will know exactly by what means the products of this country will be carried to the ports of shipment. Coming from an agricultural district, there is one question that interests me still more immediately and it is as regards what is to be done for the people who seem to me-and probably I differ from some hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House in this regard-the backbone and stay of the Dominion of Canada. The class to which I refer are the farmers. What, in the budget speech is done for the farmer, what is done to give recognition and encouragement to the efforts which the farmers are putting forth for the development of the country ? There is not one step taken to benefit the farmer or to give him any encouragement. Oh, but, I am wrong ! There is something. Why, the farmer is allowed a benefit, percolating through the men who will build a factory to grind up the sugar beet. The farmer has received a concession at the hands of the present administration and the farmer should ask no more, but should be grateful accordingly. In

order to encourage the beet-root sugar industry and so to benefit the farmers, the government have decided, as the only change that they will make in the tariff since 1897, that they will allow machinery to come in free for the period of one year. I congratulate, as congratulations are the order of the day, the farmers upon the magnificent treatment they have received from the present administration.
Now, I want to refer to some of the hon. gentlemen who have spoken, but, as the hour is getting late, and as these hon. gentlemen have all absented themselves, I am not going into it as extensively as I intended to. The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), who is a very eloquent speaker, made some remarks that I think deserves a passing reference. He compared the resolutions brought in by the Conservative opposition to ' the emergency rations.' I want to tell that hon. gentleman, and I want to tell those who cheered the allusion, that whatever divergence of opinion we may have as regards the difficulty that arose over the emergency rations to South Africa, it does not come well from that side of the House to refer to that question in this way. I cannot say whether, in the inception of that matter the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence was to blame. That is a debatable question. But, I am here to say, and I say it with a feeling ol' the full responsibility, that the government cannot be acquitted of blame in this, that when the difficulty had been shown to them, when the wrong had been shown to have been perpetrated, when it had been shown that a crime, than which it would be difficult to find one more dastardly, had been committed with reference to our brave soldier boys in South Africa, there was a duty cast upon the government and that duty has not been discharged. Therefore, I say, it does not become the hon. member for South Wellington or "any other hon. gentleman on that side of the House to say any more about emergency rations than they cau help. Now, these hon. gentlemen differ so much amongst themselves as to what the policy of the government is that it is probably better to let them fight it out amongst themselves.
